editorial.headline: Refractory Building Materials with a Clear Bali Path
editorial.standfirst: This activity covers the manufacture of refractory bricks, mortar, cement, concrete, and similar composites, open nationally to PMA and not blocked in Bali.
editorial.body:
**KBLI 23911 is a manufacturing category for materials built to withstand fire and high heat.** Its scope is not ordinary brickmaking or general cement trade; it is specifically the production of refractory bricks, refractory mortar, refractory cement, refractory concrete, and similar refractory composites. The record names alumina, silica, and basic or alkaline materials as examples, which places the activity in a technical industrial lane: products whose defining feature is resistance to fire, rather than decorative finish, structural form, or retail use.

The registration profile is unusually broad across business scale. The activity is open to micro, small, medium, and large operators, so the same code can describe a small producer making refractory mortar as well as a larger industrial operation producing refractory concrete or composite materials. That breadth matters editorially because the code is defined by the nature of the product, not by the size of the enterprise. A founder reading it should focus first on whether the planned output is genuinely refractory brick, mortar, cement, concrete, or a similar heat-resistant composite, because that is the substance of the classification.

At the national level, the stance on foreign investment is clear. The activity is marked TERBUKA, and the recorded maximum foreign ownership is 100%. In plain English, the national record treats this as open to PMA without a foreign-share cap below full ownership. The national position is sourced to Perpres 10/2021, 49/2021. There is no basis in the slim record to add a minimum capital figure, extra licensing condition, special tax point, or operational threshold, so those questions sit outside this editorial. What the record does say is enough: as a national PMA classification, this activity is open at the recorded ceiling.

Bali does not reverse that position. The province’s moratorium rule blocks all Low and Medium-Low risk activities for PMA on an island-wide, permanent basis, but this record states that KBLI 23911 is not blocked. The reason is specific: at large scale, the OSS risk is Menengah-Tinggi/Tinggi, so it is not caught by that moratorium. That does not turn the category into a casual administrative choice; it simply means the Bali-side status is not a PMA registration block under the stated moratorium rule. The honest conclusion is therefore clean: for foreign-owned setups, this refractory-materials manufacturing activity is nationally open up to 100% foreign ownership and, on the record provided, remains registrable in Bali rather than barred by the provincial PMA moratorium.
